name: Alex Pico · xanderpico
description: Alex Pico is an experimental scientist and software builder with a background in materials science, neuroscience, protein structure and function, bioinformatics, and collaborative disease research. Exploring AI and complex systems.
about: Threads are ongoing projects. Each thread has resources (articles, results, tables, trackers, newsletters) and records (outside sources it draws on). Every thread and resource page has a Markdown copy at the listed address.

threads.title: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
threads.guiding_question: Where do the quick judgments of a very cheap AI differ from ours, and what does running thousands of tests teach us about minds and about building with AI?
threads.summary: Jev, from TypeSafe AI, answers a typed question about a text with a probability in about a fifth of a second for about two thousandths of a cent, and when it is confident it gives the same answer each time. That makes psychology-style experiments practical at a scale that normally needs hundreds of volunteers: rating thousands of words, or running a battery of classic bias tests in minutes. What turns up matters to AI builders, Jev users and brain researchers: some human quirks appear, some do not, and on first impressions it does the opposite of people.

findings.text: With bad facts about a job candidate listed last, Jev's rating was 0.82 points lower on a 9-point scale in 12 of 12 sets, the reverse of people's first-impression pattern.
Rated one at a time, Jev scored the conjunction higher on all 20 Linda-style profiles; shown both statements side by side, it picked the conjunction on none.
A random anchor number moved Jev's estimates 0.7 points on a 0–100 scale for facts it knows, and 8.6 points for things it cannot know.
Jev's word ratings correlated with human norms at 0.90 for concreteness and 0.88 for valence, but only 0.61 for arousal, and rewording did not repair arousal.
Across the 999 SimLex-999 word pairs, Jev's similarity ratings correlated 0.854 with people's ratings, though its scores were usually lower.
On 600 words, Jev matched human sensory ratings best for touch (0.783) and worst for interoception, the inner-body sense (0.494).
The whole bias battery took 1,356 calls and cost $0.0225; the word-rating work took 12,740 calls and cost $0.22.

threads.limits: Results cover one pinned model version, prompts written for this work, and about a dozen items in many bias tests; they do not compare Jev with other models or show shared human mechanisms.

related_threads.why: Both run experiments on Jev, TypeSafe AI's judgment model: one compares its judgments with people's, the other uses them as logic gates.

threads.title: Frontier labs as national laboratories
threads.guiding_question: As national security and international competition press on the frontier AI labs, which past model of a national laboratory do they come to resemble, and where does the comparison break down?
threads.summary: An essay on whether national security, secure methods and international competition will push the frontier AI labs toward national-laboratory status, and what past labs suggest about the shape that could take.

findings.text: As of the 2026-11-12 snapshot, the highest estimate is 90% (range 80–96%) that ad hoc levers continue, the status quo, through 2030.
Steering through conditions on chips and contracts is estimated at 82% (range 62–92%) by 2030, as of the 2026-11-12 snapshot.
Frontier labs as users and partners of national facilities is estimated at 60% (range 45–75%) by 2030, as of the 2026-11-12 snapshot.
A national-champion bargain, with protection and procurement in exchange for a public return, is estimated at 35% (range 20–52%) by 2030, as of the 2026-11-12 snapshot.
An AI FFRDC under an M&O contract, where the government owns a secure AI facility and contracts an operator, is estimated at 20% (range 8–35%), as of the 2026-11-12 snapshot.
A national laboratory is a government-owned facility run by a contractor the government can grade and replace; the Department of Energy has 17, with 16 under management-and-operating contracts.

threads.limits: The probabilities are judgment-based estimates that can co-occur and do not sum to 100%; the March, June and September 2026 points are simulated retrospective estimates, not measurements made at the time.

threads.title: AI-native biology, beyond the announcements
threads.guiding_question: What are AI-native biotech companies betting on, how do their approaches differ, and what changes as the work meets reality?
threads.summary: A research series on the companies rebuilding biological discovery around AI: what they are betting on, how their approaches differ, and what changes as the work meets reality.

findings.text: Four AI-first drug discovery companies (BigHat, Genesis, Absci, Manas AI) name accuracy in molecule design as the scarce thing while owning very different labs; Recursion's executive names target choice instead.
Of 15 Recursion statements scored against the company's later statements, 7 were marked met, mostly milestones the company largely controls.
Recursion's CEO said in 2024 that its pipeline would have 100 programs; its FY2025 annual report says up to 40 small molecule programs over a decade or longer.
Recursion said 13 of 15 evaluable patients had a deep reduction in polyp burden after 12 weeks on REC-4881; the page notes no described comparison group.
Recursion, Relay, Schrödinger and Absci have each moved at least one program toward a partner or a spin-out this year or last, as of the Q3 2026 comparison.
Among the speed and efficiency claims in the four companies' Q3 2026 documents, one names its comparison: Recursion's 204 compounds against about 2,500.
Relay's annual reports moved its stated cash runway from into 2025 to into 2029, while the cash figure in the same sentence went from $998.9 million to $554.5 million.

threads.limits: Entries are machine-selected and not reviewed by a person, and plans are compared with each company's later statements, not with trial results; the pages are research and commentary, not investment advice.

threads.title: Growing up with AI
threads.guiding_question: What should kids and teens practice for themselves and what can they hand to AI, and what does the evidence say so far?
threads.summary: An essay of advice for kids, teens and future generations growing up with powerful AI.

findings.text: AI can take over routine tasks, but the thinking, writing and struggling that build a child's abilities should stay with the child.
In a high-school math study, students with open GPT-4 access scored about 48% higher on practice problems, then about 17% worse once the AI was removed.
Broad skills such as learning new tools, adapting to new circumstances and taking initiative are recommended as a hedge against an uncertain AI future.
Asking "how do you know?" and checking a second source is the suggested habit, because AI answers almost anything instantly and is sometimes confidently wrong.
A national survey found 72% of US teens aged 13-17 have used an AI companion, and about one in three found those conversations as satisfying as talking with friends.

threads.limits: The section on friends, making things and data is presented as personal conviction that the quoted experts do not argue, though research is said to support it.

resources.title: Weightlifting, Not Forklifting: Advice for Growing Up with AI
resources.summary: Nobody knows what the AI future looks like, so don't bet a kid's childhood on one version of it. Five rules for parents and mentors that hold up either way: keep the workouts, hedge, ask how do you know, protect the human parts, and don't panic.

threads.summary: An independent experiment that uses a Jev Boolean judgment as the only logic primitive for gates, an SR latch, and Rule 110 cell updates, with recorded runs and a ground-truth checker. It is not affiliated with TypeSafe AI or Vercel.

related_threads.why: Both run experiments on Jev, TypeSafe AI's judgment model: one compares its judgments with people's, the other uses them as logic gates.

records.title: Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
records.why: Cook's paper gives a proof that Rule 110 is capable of universal computation and states the binary nearest-neighbor update rule used by the experiment's ground-truth checker.

records.title: Statistical mechanics of cellular automata
records.why: Wolfram's paper analyzes elementary cellular automata with binary sites that update from nearest neighbors in discrete time, the rule family from which Rule 110 is drawn.

records.title: Probabilistic logics and the synthesis of reliable organisms from unreliable components
records.why: von Neumann treats error as an essential part of automata synthesis and frames networks as connected basic components with finite time delays. It is the source the project cites for making an explicit error budget and for distinguishing a noisy voter from the gate it votes over.

threads.title: The wave and the leash
threads.guiding_question: Who should count the failures when people hand more of what they do to AI, and how can anyone tell that the counting is independent of the thing being counted?
threads.summary: An essay on the long line of capacities people have handed to tools and institutions, why most of us will not refuse the next handoff to AI, and who should independently count its failures. Includes Who counts?, a quarterly ledger of how AI is being checked.

resources.title: The wave and the leash
resources.summary: People have always handed parts of their lives to things bigger and faster than any one of us. AI may be the first handoff to reach the whole loop of sensing, remembering, learning, deciding and acting. Most people will not refuse it, so the practical question is who counts its failures, independently of the thing counted.

resources.title: Who counts? A ledger of how AI is checked
resources.summary: For each standard, law, company framework, research method, tribunal ruling and insurance product that checks AI: who writes the definitions, who pays the checker, when the authority ends, whose evidence is used and what the checker loses if wrong. Quotations and links only, no grades. Refreshed quarterly.

threads.title: Passwords in the Age of AI
threads.guiding_question: Which everyday habits matter most for keeping accounts safe now that AI makes familiar scams cheaper to run?
threads.summary: A four-page, printable guide for friends and family on keeping accounts safe now that AI makes familiar scams easier: the five ways accounts get opened, password managers and passkeys, a security-key setup, recovery, and a worksheet for the accounts everything else depends on.

findings.text: A password manager should generate and autofill a different password for every account, with at least 20 random characters where the website allows it.
Caller ID, tone and personal details do not prove who is calling, because AI can imitate writing or a familiar voice.
An old phone number, recovery email, support process or carrier account can bypass a strong sign-in, so recovery methods need to be kept current and tested.
Each security key, including the spare, should be tested after signing out, because a spare that was never registered will not restore access.
Changing a password may not end an existing signed-in session, so other sessions and unknown devices also need to be removed after a suspected compromise.

resources.title: Passwords in the Age of AI: a friends and family guide
resources.summary: A four-page, printable guide to keeping accounts safe now that AI makes familiar scams easier. August 2026.

threads.title: Scale Tool
threads.guiding_question: What can a single number mean when it is compared, without false equivalence, across quantities such as time, distance, mass, energy, information, and temperature?
threads.summary: A React and TypeScript explorer in which one editable decimal value drives source-backed comparisons across nine distinct units. It keeps estimates, models, theory, and unknown quantities explicitly separate from measurements.

records.title: SI Units
records.why: NIST explains that the SI rests on seven defining constants and lists its seven base units, providing the unit framework for comparisons that must not equate unlike quantities.

records.title: Sun Fact Sheet
records.why: NASA's fact sheet gives the Sun's mass, radius, luminosity, surface gravity, and other parameters, illustrating the source-backed physical comparisons a scale tool can present.

records.title: Resolution 3 of the 27th CGPM (2022): On the extension of the range of SI prefixes
records.why: The CGPM added ronna, ronto, quetta, and quecto as SI prefixes, citing the need to express digital-information quantities beyond 10^24.

records.title: Planck 2018 results - VI. Cosmological parameters
records.why: The Planck Collaboration's final full-mission analysis reports a base-ΛCDM Hubble constant of 67.4 ± 0.5 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ and matter density parameter Ωm = 0.315 ± 0.007. Scale Tool's expansion-cosmology model uses those rounded inputs.
